text:
Two years of hard labor for looking at a white girl. That was the sentence a North Carolina judge handed Mack Ingram in 1951, and the girl herself testified in three separate courtrooms that he never touched her and never made a move to come closer. He was about seventy feet away, walking a neighbor's field to ask her father about borrowing a hay trailer.

There is a sentence in the North Carolina law reports about a cluster of plum bushes.

It sits in a bound volume that lawyers still pull down off the shelf. Those bushes are preserved in the permanent legal record of a state because one man stopped walking beside them on a June morning, and North Carolina then spent twenty months trying to prove that stopping there was a crime.

His name was Mack Ingram. Some records and some of the scholarship call him Matt, and the wire photograph taken during his trial ran him as Matt "Mack" Ingram, but his grave marker at Sassafras Grove reads James Mack Ingram.

He was forty-four years old, a Black tenant farmer in Caswell County, up against the Virginia line. He and his wife Linward had nine children.

By the standards of that place and that year, he was doing well. He owned his own tools, his own equipment, mules on the property, and an old automobile he drove around town.

He was better off than a good many of the white people in Yanceyville. In a segregated tobacco county in 1951 everybody could see that, and it matters later.

The white locals in that town had a phrase for him before any of this started. He was a good Negro, they said, meaning he did not cause trouble.

One morning in June 1951 he had hay to move and no trailer to move it in.

So he drove around to a few houses in the area asking to borrow one. One of the places he stopped was the Boswell farm, because he wanted to ask Willa Jean Boswell's father about using their equipment.

Nobody was home.

So he started walking the property to find Mr. Boswell. Nobody involved in this case ever said that was strange, because the Boswells knew Ingram and he had been to that house before.

He went into the woods near the property. Up ahead on the path he saw someone walking toward the family's tobacco field with a hoe in hand.

The Supreme Court would later count that walk in steps. Ninety-five.

He stopped at a cluster of plum bushes at the edge of the cultivated ground, sixty-five or seventy feet away by the state's own account.

He did not go any further. He turned around and headed back toward the road.

He never did find Mr. Boswell. So he drove to a second farm, borrowed a trailer there, drove to a third farm, and he was loading hay on that property when the police came and arrested him.

The person on the path had been Willa Jean Boswell, seventeen years old, on her way out to join her father and brothers in the tobacco field.

Her account and his do not conflict much, which is the strangest thing about this entire case.

She said she had seen Ingram driving along the dirt road earlier and that he slowed as he passed her and put his head out the window to look at her. She said that frightened her, and she kept walking, and then she saw him coming toward her in the woods.

She said he stopped about sixty-five or seventy feet away, then turned back toward the road.

She said he never touched her. She said he never made a motion to come closer, and she told three separate courts the same thing.

She reached her family and cried. Her father and brothers called the police, and Mack Ingram was arrested that afternoon and charged with assault with intent to commit rape.

There is a name for what he was accused of, and people have called it reckless eyeballing ever since. It is worth knowing that no such law ever existed.

It was never a statute in North Carolina or anywhere else. There was nothing on the books to challenge, nothing to repeal, and nothing a lawyer could hold up and call unconstitutional.

That is what made it usable. It lived inside the ordinary law of assault, where any prosecutor who wanted it could reach in and pick it up.

He was arraigned in Caswell County and waited for trial in jail.

His wife was pregnant that summer. Linward and their eleven year old son worked the fields and kept the farm alive while he sat there, because the people of Yanceyville had already turned on the family.

A local white lawyer took the case. E. Frederick Upchurch was seventy-six years old and well respected in the county, and it is believed Ingram went to him personally, knowing the man and having no money for a lawyer.

Upchurch arranged bail at fifteen hundred dollars.

Then he went to the courthouse to post it, and the prosecutor asked the judge to raise the figure. The judge raised it to eighteen hundred.

The first trial was held in Caswell County Recorder's Court. The judge, Ralph Vernon, was a local farmer with no legal training.

Willa Jean took the stand and tearfully described being afraid when she saw Ingram looking at her.

The prosecutor was W. Banks Horton, and he did not argue the facts so much as the fear underneath them. He said out loud, in that courtroom, that young womanhood had to be protected from Black men, and he used a slur to say it.

Vernon told Horton to drop the rape charge. An earlier state supreme court decision had already held that an assault with no physical contact could not be charged as rape, so the law would not carry it.

So the charge came down to assault on a female. Vernon convicted him and gave him the maximum, two years.

Ingram's lawyers appealed immediately.

The case caught national attention, and that is the only reason there is a record of him at all.

The NAACP heard about it and sent two Black attorneys with backgrounds in desegregation work. The Civil Rights Congress, a group with Communist Party ties, ran its own loud campaign in the Daily Worker and organized letter writing into North Carolina.

One of those headlines named the thing nobody in that courthouse would say out loud. Negro Was Framed For Doing Too Well On Farm.

That is the part to sit with. A Black tenant farmer in a segregated county owned his own mules and his own car and was doing better than his white neighbors, and then a look put him in a cell.

The NAACP hated the tactics, convinced that kind of noise only hardened white officials against the men they were trying to save. They may have been right, and the noise is still the reason this case survived at all.

His appeal went before a Superior Court grand jury first. Eighteen people, all white, and they returned an indictment for assault with intent to rape, putting the charge Vernon had already dropped right back on him.

The second trial came in November 1951, in front of a jury of eight white men and four Black men.

A jury with four Black men seated on it, in Caswell County, in 1951, was close to unheard of. That jury could not reach a verdict, and the judge declared a mistrial.

What happened inside that room was never written down. Twelve men went in, they could not agree, and Mack Ingram walked back out of that courthouse because of it.

The prosecutor renewed the charge and set him for trial a third time.

In November 1952, seventeen months after he went out to borrow a trailer, Mack Ingram went before an all-white jury.

His lawyers asked for a change of venue, because the local papers had already decided he was guilty in print. Judge Frank Armstrong refused.

His lawyers then put the jury itself on the record. Caswell County was forty-nine percent Black, and the pool of seventy-six people this jury had been drawn from was somehow entirely white.

Armstrong denied that motion too, along with every other motion the defense made.

At trial, Willa Jean testified that she recognized Ingram when she saw him. Her father testified that he knew Ingram as well.

Both of them acknowledged that it was normal for Ingram to be traveling that route, because he visited other homes in the community. And Willa Jean again confirmed that he never touched her and never made a motion to come closer.

That was the state's case. A man everyone knew, on a road he had every reason to be on, who did nothing.

Then Armstrong charged the jury, and what he said is worth reading slowly.

He instructed them that it is not always necessary for there to be physical contact with the person alleged to have been assaulted. He told them that if a man looks at someone in a leering manner, sly or threatening or suggestive, and watches her and then follows her, and causes her to become frightened and run or to do something other than what she would have done, then he is guilty of assault.

That instruction is the entire theory of reckless eyeballing, spoken from a bench, as law, in 1952. Ingram's lawyers objected and Armstrong overruled them.

Then Armstrong told the jury the opposite. He said they had to acquit if all Ingram did was look at her in a threatening or suggestive way.

The court solicitor got up, walked to the bench, and whispered to him.

Armstrong turned back to the jury and told them that under the last instruction, if he had said they would find him guilty, they were to disabuse their minds of that, because the court had intended to say not guilty.

So the jury had been told that a look was a crime, that a look was not a crime, and that the judge had misspoken about which. They convicted Mack Ingram anyway.

Nobody in that room was confused about the law. They were never deciding the law.

Armstrong sentenced him to six months with physical labor, then suspended it for five years. To keep it suspended, Ingram had to pay the court fees, stay on good behavior, break no laws, and appear in person at each November term of court to prove by himself and by witnesses that he had kept every one of those terms.

His lawyers appealed again, on the contradictory instructions, the refused venue change, and the all-white jury in a county that was half Black. The North Carolina Supreme Court agreed to hear it.

On February 25, 1953, Chief Justice William A. Devin took the entire thing apart.

He went back through a century of state decisions on what an assault is and laid out the requirement that had always been there, which is an overt act, an offer or an attempt to do physical injury.

Then he held the state's own witness up against that standard.

She had used the word leer. The dictionary gives that word a sly and lustful edge, and Devin noted it, and then he noted what the witness herself said when she was asked what she meant by it.

She said it meant a curious look. Nothing further, no explanation, no demonstration.

That she was frightened was not in question, the court said. But fear alone does not make an assault when there is no menace of violence behind it.

He made no sound and no gesture. He turned and walked back the way he came.

Then came the line. What may have been in his mind is not something human law reaches.

The conviction was reversed. The case should have been thrown out before it ever went to a jury.

The court did not hand him a clean acquittal, though, and this part deserves saying plainly. In that same opinion the justices remarked that his stated reason for crossing the field was rather lame, and allowed that he may well have looked at her with lustful eyes.

They cleared him without ever deciding to believe him.

There is one more passage in that opinion that people skip past. The court declined to rule on whether Caswell County had deliberately kept Black men off its juries.

But it went out of its way to note that the county commissioners had not been following the jury statute. They had been drawing names from the election registration books instead of the tax records the law specified.

In a county that was nearly half Black, in a state where Black registration was strangled at the registrar's desk, that was not a clerical preference. The court observed that careful attention to the statute would do much to improve the quality of juries in North Carolina.

That was the remedy. An observation.

Mack Ingram was cleared of everything, and it did not give him his life back.

The farmers around Yanceyville who had hired him before were now afraid to, because standing near his name would cost them their own reputations. The work went away.

So he sold off the farming equipment he owned to keep his family fed.

Go back to the beginning of this and understand what that means. The equipment was the reason he had been doing better than his white neighbors in the first place.

It was the exact thing that headline had named. He was doing too well on that farm, and by the time the state was finished with him, he was not.

While the case was in the papers, strangers sent the family money and clothes. When the papers moved on, that stopped too.

The Ingrams were still shut out of Yanceyville after the state's highest court cleared him. They took their business across the line to Danville, Virginia, instead.

Mack Ingram died in 1973. Linward outlived him by thirty years and died in 2003.

Four years after his arrest, a fourteen year old named Emmett Till was killed in Mississippi over an accusation of the same kind. Ingram had the courts and the newspapers and a chief justice on his side, and he still lost everything he owned.

The case itself was never forgotten. State versus Ingram sits in the North Carolina reports as a clean statement of what an assault requires, and lawyers cite it who have no idea whose life is underneath it.

The plum bushes are in there. The sixty-five or seventy feet are in there, and the ninety-five steps are counted and preserved, permanently, in the law of the state.

What the volume does not record is the trailer.

He borrowed one from a farmer down the road that same morning and got his hay in. That was the last thing in this entire story that went the way Mack Ingram planned it.

The law books kept the plum bushes and lost the man standing beside them. He is not hard to pick back up.

He was forty-four years old. He had nine children and a wife named Linward, he owned his own mules and his own car in a county that could not stand it, and on a June morning in 1951 he walked ninety-five steps across a field to ask a neighbor about borrowing a trailer.

Every coffee helps me keep creating.
Matt Ingram's name ended up in law books, but the real story was the farmer, husband, and father whose life changed because of a moment in a cornfield. I share stories like his because history is not only made in famous places. Sometimes it happens to ordinary people who were forced to stand their ground.

Peace is durable when aggression realizes there's no favorable cost-benefit calculation. 

An expanded Starlink coverage would increase the defender's ability to hunt the aggressor's launch systems. 

"An ally helps Ukraine defeat the aggressor, rather than haggling with it over the right to defend itself." 

Which is precisely why it's objectionable to have to trade away refinery strikes to obtain it.

Denys Shtilierman on X: 

An editorial entitled ‘Zelensky Is Open to a Starlink Deal’ has been published in WSJ Opinion. And I completely disagree with the main message of this piece.  

The WSJ is proposing a deal to Ukraine: we would halt strikes on Russian energy infrastructure for 100 days, and in return the US would extend Starlink coverage approximately 300 kilometres into Russia, so that the Ukrainian army could strike missile launchers and drones.  

According to the WSJ, this proposal was conveyed to Zelenskyy by Republican Senators Roger Wicker and Kevin Cramer.  

The editorial states:  

“Ukraine would take a breather from striking Russian energy assets. In exchange the U.S. would expand Ukraine’s Starlink satellite coverage up to roughly 300 kilometers into Russia.”  

And further:  

“The trade by our lights is worth it.”  

In my opinion, no. This is not how relations between allies should look.  

Such a deal might at least resemble a fair one if Ukraine were given the full capacity to operate up to 470 kilometres deep into Russia, rather than just 300.

Kharkiv is situated approximately 30 kilometres from the Russian border, Sumy approximately 25–30 kilometres, and Kyiv just over 200 kilometres. Meanwhile, Russia can launch missiles from territory situated considerably further than the proposed 300-kilometre zone.  

Therefore, 300 kilometres does not represent parity. It is yet another artificial restriction on Ukraine’s capabilities. A range of up to 470 kilometres would at least have allowed for a significant expansion of the zone within which Russian launchers could not operate with impunity.  

First, Starlink and Starshield – which are critically important to the Ukrainian army – are restricted without warning. Such decisions cost Ukrainian lives. Then Ukraine is offered the chance to restore or expand these capabilities in exchange for refraining from strikes on one of the most vulnerable points of the Russian military economy.  

This is not a deal. It is blackmail.  At the same time, the WSJ itself acknowledges the obvious:  

“Ukraine has every right to raise the pressure on Mr. Putin to stop his conquest.”  

This raises a simple question: if Ukraine has this right, why should it have to pay the price of refraining from effective strikes in exchange for the ability to defend itself against Russian missiles?  

“But the ability to hit the Russian archer instead of letting the arrows fall is even better.” 

But the mere ability to strike at the “archer” must not come at the cost of security guarantees for Russian oil refineries.  

Ukraine needs both the ability to destroy Russian launchers and the ability to strike at the infrastructure that sustains the Russian war machine.  

For some reason, Russia isn’t making a choice. Why should Ukraine have to choose?

Especially after Trump had already announced some sort of ‘energy truce’ – one that Ukraine and Russia had not, in fact, agreed upon between themselves – whilst Russia continued its strikes.

“A frustrated Mr. Zelensky now says Ukraine will resume targeting Russian energy sites after Mr. Putin ignored Mr. Trump’s announcement last weekend of a “cease-fire” and continued to bomb Ukraine’s energy sites.”

Russia is violating the ‘ceasefire’. Russia continues to strike. Yet once again, Ukraine is being asked to make concessions.  

No.

America has been and remains our ally. The American people, Congress, the military and millions of Americans have helped Ukraine throughout the war. That is precisely why, as a matter of principle, I do not wish to equate the United States with the current administration.

Through its recent actions, the current US administration is behaving not as an ally of Ukraine, but as an ally of Russia.  

We hope that the American political system will be able to restore relations between the US and Ukraine to a normal alliance model.  

Because the normal model is very simple.  

Russia is the aggressor.  

Ukraine is defending itself.

An ally helps Ukraine defeat the aggressor, rather than haggling with it over the right to defend itself.

More importantly—what are you doing?

You call it rioting. I call it warfare on the streets of our cities—and another appearance on television is not going to stop it.

Police are not soldiers. Stop asking them to carry a military burden while you offer them praise as though praise were protection.

Your praise and a penny won’t buy them a cup of coffee. It certainly won’t keep them safe.

Where is the military? Where is the leadership?

Enough meetings on Monday. Enough photo ops. Enough looking like you mean business while everyone waits for you to actually mean it.

And the EU? I have no confidence in that lot—ideologues who, to my mind, have mistaken appeasement for leadership. Waiting for Brussels is not a strategy. It is another excuse.

France should be the warning—not the example Italy follows into the same disaster.

Leave this violence unchecked and my fear is that the fire will spread from city to city—straight to Rome while you are still discussing how to respond.

Madam President—or whatever your title is—the title means nothing if you will not carry the responsibility.

An authoritative voice on television is not action. Looking determined is not a decision.

**BASTA.**

I am calling for military intervention—not another speech. Deploy the Army, under lawful orders, to support overwhelmed police and protect the public.

This is war as I see it. Stop treating it as a public-relations problem.

You have a military. Use it—before the emergency you keep talking about becomes the catastrophe you failed to stop.

Rough week for tech. The Nasdaq 100 fell 5.5%, its worst week since April 2025, and chips dropped eight days in a row. Yet the S&P is only about 2% off its high.

The market’s derisking and dumping AI that runs on borrowed money.

Look at who's still winning this year. $SNDK is up 488% and $MU 226%, both paying for growth out of their own cash. Power names like $BE and $GEV became the build-out trade. Energy is the top sector, led by refiners like $MPC (+197%) and $VLO (+177%).

I break this down in my article here:

https://t.co/zZ6kCqjxis

Now look at who's breaking. $CRWV fell more than 20% this week, and the cost to insure its debt against default is above 1,000bp. That's the market saying it's not sure all this borrowing gets paid back.

Underneath the index it's worse than it looks. About 60% of S&P stocks are down 20% or more from their highs. Two groups are basically holding everything up, and if one of them cracks, there isn't much underneath.

The weekend didn't clear anything up. Iran's Guard claims tankers hit mines in Hormuz, which nobody has confirmed. At the same time, Iran's offer to reopen the strait in seven days is still on the table. Oil could gap either way Monday. TSMC and ASML say chip demand is strong, but reports say Anthropic's growth slowed sharply. If that's real, it's the first crack on the demand side, not just the debt side.

What I'm watching this week:
• Wednesday: the 20-year Treasury auction, plus $META and $TSLA earnings. That's the real test of AI spending.
• Thursday: $VLO , for a read on refining margins.
• The VIX. A close above 20 with oil above $110 is where I get defensive. Real panic, the kind worth buying, usually means a VIX above 30. We're not there.

My take: this is a market rotation sorting companies by their balance sheets, not a crash-yet. I'd rather own the cash generators until uncertainty clears.

(A) Generally no, as freedom of speech must be protected. However, strict restrictions can be justified in exceptional cases, such as preventing hate speech, terrorism, or severe misinformation that directly threatens public safety.

Under The Media Man Watercooler

Past, Present And Future

(ICYMI)

The world's top sports brands include Nike, Adidas, Lululemon, Puma, and Under Armour.

These brands dominate the market in terms of revenue, brand value, and global recognition. Nike consistently ranks as the most valuable sports brand, followed by Adidas, with a significant gap in brand value.

The List

Nike: A global leader in athletic footwear, apparel, and equipment, known for its iconic swoosh logo and strong brand recognition.

Adidas: A major competitor to Nike, offering a wide range of sports apparel, footwear, and accessories.

Lululemon: Specializing in athletic apparel, particularly yoga wear, but expanding into other areas like running shoes and personal care.

Puma: A well-known sportswear brand with a strong presence in football and other sports.

Under Armour: A prominent brand known for its performance apparel and innovative technologies.

Other notable brands: ASICS, Fila, New Balance, Skechers, Decathlon, and more, each with their own niche in the market.

News Flashback

Sports Brands: News

Nike: Nike has launched a new soccer campaign, “Scary Good,” focusing on talented players redefining the sport. This aligns with their “Sport Offense” strategy, emphasizing performance wear and storytelling in key sports like running and basketball, following a quarter of underwhelming financial results. CEO Elliott Hill aims to differentiate Nike, Jordan Brand, and Converse by sport for sharper brand distinction. Additionally, tennis player Carlos Alcaraz debuted Nike’s retro-inspired 2025 London Collection cardigan at Wimbledon, blending classic tennis tradition with modern flair.

New Balance: The 119-year-old brand is making waves by signing young superstars like Cooper Flagg, Shohei Ohtani, and Coco Gauff, aiming to redefine its position in the sports hierarchy. This move has shifted its image from “dad shoe” to a top contender, notably with Flagg as the No. 1 NBA Draft prospect.

Adidas: Adidas unveiled the new Team India T20 jersey, available since May 2024, ahead of the T20 World Cup, reinforcing its presence in cricket sponsorships.

JD Sports Fashion: As a global omnichannel retailer, JD Sports continues to expand its portfolio, including brands like Nike, Adidas, and The North Face, alongside private labels like Pink Soda. Its segments include DTLR, Shoe Palace, and Sizeer, focusing on athletic footwear and apparel with strong community ties.

Grassroots Sports Marketing: Brands are increasingly investing in grassroots sports for deeper emotional connections. In India, non-cricket sports sponsorships surpassed ₹2,000 crore in 2023, with platforms like SportVot boosting grassroots athletes’ visibility through digital identities and streaming lesser-known sports.

Other Developments: Athleta, a Gap-owned brand, has partnered with female athletes like Katie Ledecky and Simone Biles, pioneering sports marketing in women’s sports. Sephora’s sponsorship of the WNBA’s Golden State Valkyries signals growing brand interest in women’s sports. Meanwhile, brands like Red Lobster and Ram are leveraging CEOs in campaigns tied to smaller sports markets for affordable, intimate marketing.

Several well-known brands dominate the combat sports market, offering a wide range of equipment and apparel for various disciplines. Some of the most popular brands include Venum, Adidas, Everlast, Fairtex, Hayabusa, Rival, and Ringside. These brands are recognized for their quality, innovation, and unique designs, catering to both professional athletes and enthusiasts.

Media

Combat Sports Brands

These brands cater to various combat sports, offering specialized gear for different disciplines and skill levels. For beginners, brands like Everlast and RDX Sports are budget-friendly, while Hayabusa and Fairtex appeal to advanced practitioners seeking premium quality. Always consider your discipline, budget, and needs (e.g., durability, fit) when choosing gear. Venum: A leading brand since 2006, known for durable, stylish gear for MMA, boxing, BJJ, and karate. Became the UFC’s exclusive outfitting partner in 2021, offering gloves, shorts, and rashguards. Popular for innovative designs and high-quality materials.

Hayabusa: A premium brand specializing in MMA, boxing, and BJJ gear. Known for advanced technology, ergonomic designs, and durable gloves, shin guards, and training equipment. Highly regarded for performance and comfort.

Fairtex: A renowned Thai brand focused on Muay Thai and MMA gear, particularly gloves and shin guards. Trusted for durability and quality, widely used by Muay Thai practitioners.

Combat Sports International: Offers affordable, high-quality MMA gear, including gloves, grappling dummies, and heavy bags. Based in Kansas City, known for innovation and catering to all skill levels.

Everlast: A household name in boxing, also offering MMA and fitness gear. Known for reliable, durable equipment like gloves and protective gear, suitable for beginners and pros.

Adidas Combat Sports: Brings the iconic athletic brand into martial arts, offering gear for judo, taekwondo, and MMA. Known for quality and versatility, with a focus on fitness enthusiasts.

Fuji Sports: A top choice for BJJ and judo, known for high-quality gis that prioritize comfort and fit. Favored by grapplers for durability and performance.

Twins Special: Another Thai brand excelling in Muay Thai and MMA gear, particularly gloves and shin guards. Renowned for durability and quality, a go-to for striking arts.

Leone 1947: An Italian brand specializing in boxing and kickboxing gear, offering affordable, high-quality gloves, shin guards, and accessories. Popular among professional fighters.

Elite Sports: Offers affordable, premium-quality fight wear for BJJ, MMA, boxing, and more. Known for stylish gis, rashguards, and gloves, catering to men, women, and kids.

Revgear: A California-based brand since 1996, recognized for innovative, durable equipment for boxing, MMA, Muay Thai, and BJJ. Trusted by athletes for high-performance gear. (Grok)

Sports Promoters: Brands

Sports promoters are critical in bridging brands like Nike, Adidas, Red Bull, and emerging players like YouTube with sports ecosystems. They craft partnerships that resonate with fans, leveraging events, athletes, and digital platforms to drive engagement and revenue. For brands seeking to enter or expand in sports, working with agencies like Octagon, SPORTFIVE, or rEvolution ensures strategic alignment and impactful campaigns.

Sports promoters are key players in connecting brands with sports events, athletes, and fans to create mutually beneficial partnerships. They facilitate sponsorships, endorsements, and marketing campaigns that amplify brand visibility while enhancing the sports experience. Below is an overview of notable brands involved in sports promotion, based on their prominence in the industry and partnerships, as well as the role of sports promoters in these collaborations.

Key Brands in Sports Promotion

Sports promoters often work with global brands across various industries, leveraging the emotional and cultural appeal of sports to drive engagement. Some prominent brands include:

Nike: A leader in sports marketing, Nike partners with athletes and teams worldwide, using campaigns like #BetterForIt to promote inclusivity and fitness through influencer and athlete endorsements.

Example: Nike’s campaigns often feature athletes as brand ambassadors, such as their work with social media influencers and everyday athletes to motivate active lifestyles. Adidas: Known for high-profile collaborations with teams, athletes, and designers, adidas merges sports and lifestyle through partnerships like those with Ivy Park, Bad Bunny, and Gucci.

Promoters facilitate these deals, ensuring alignment with events like soccer tournaments or fashion-driven campaigns. Red Bull: Specializes in extreme sports and high-energy branding, Red Bull works with promoters to create visually stunning campaigns, such as those featuring snowboarder Travis Rice, aligning with their adventurous brand image.

Promoters manage event sponsorships and athlete endorsements to maximize Red Bull’s reach. Gatorade: A staple in sports hydration, Gatorade signs college athletes like Cooper Flagg, Paige Bueckers, and JuJu Watkins for endorsement deals, expanding its influence in youth markets.

Promoters negotiate these contracts to ensure brand alignment with emerging talent. Reebok: Recently extended a multiyear endorsement with Chicago Sky’s Angel Reese, including a signature shoe release planned for 2026.

Promoters handle such deals to integrate Reebok’s branding into WNBA events and fan engagement. Under Armour, Puma, and New Balance: These brands compete in the athleisure and performance markets, often collaborating with promoters to secure sponsorships for events like marathons or partnerships with rising stars.

Example: New Balance’s revival through collaborations with designers and athletes highlights promoter-driven strategies. Non-Traditional Brands: Companies like YouTube (partnering with Mr. Beast for NBA jersey patches) and luxury brands like Hugo Boss and Gucci (F1 and tennis sponsorships) are increasingly entering sports through innovative partnerships.

Promoters bridge these brands with sports audiences, crafting campaigns that appeal to diverse demographics.

Role of Sports Promoters

Sports promoters act as intermediaries, orchestrating partnerships that benefit brands, athletes, and events.

Their roles include:

Event Promotion: Organizing and marketing events like tournaments, matches, or festivals, ensuring brands gain visibility through sponsorships (e.g., Sports Marketing Australia’s work with AusTriathlon).

Athlete Endorsements: Negotiating deals between brands and athletes, such as Jannik Sinner’s partnerships with Gucci, Nike, and Rolex. Sponsorship Activation: Creating campaigns that integrate brands into sports culture, like Starbucks and Seattle Seahawks’ co-branded merchandise.

Digital and Social Media Campaigns: Leveraging platforms for influencer-driven marketing, as seen with Nike’s #BetterForIt or Red Bull’s extreme sports content.

Global Reach: Connecting brands with international markets, such as Allsport Promotion’s campaigns for global brands across Europe and beyond.

Notable Sports Promotion

Agencies

Several agencies specialize in facilitating these brand partnerships:

Octagon: A global leader in sports and entertainment, representing talent and brands across multiple sports.

SPORTFIVE: Creates value for brands through partnerships with rights holders and media platforms.

rEvolution: Focuses on authentic campaigns that connect brands with passionate fans.

Excel Sports Management: Manages high-value contracts for athletes in basketball, baseball, and golf, with $3.4 billion in contracts.

IMG: Specializes in rights, data, and digital strategies for sports organizations and brands.

CSM: Known for creating memorable experiences through partnerships, like Red Bull Racing’s F1 activations.

Trends in Sports Promotion:

Influencer Marketing: Brands like Nike and Red Bull use athletes and influencers to create authentic, engaging content.

Sustainability and Social Causes: Over 80% of consumers prefer brands supporting environmental or diversity initiatives, prompting promoters to align brands with such values.

Non-Traditional Partnerships: Luxury and tech brands (e.g., Gucci, YouTube) are entering sports, expanding promoter opportunities.

Data-Driven Marketing: Agencies like TwoCircles use data to enhance campaign effectiveness, a growing trend in sports promotion. (Grok)

UFC Brand: News

These developments show UFC’s aggressive brand expansion through strategic partnerships, rebranding efforts, and global market penetration, solidifying its position as a dominant force in combat sports and beyond.

Pacsun Partnership at UFC International Fight Week 2025: Pacsun made its debut at UFC X during International Fight Week (June 25–29, 2025) with a branded booth and a custom Pacsun-branded step-and-repeat for fan and fighter interactions. They also had a major brand integration on the UFC X mainstage, including two athlete Q&A sessions presented by Pacsun with prominent LED logo displays. The Pacsun x UFC International Fight Week 2025 collection is available in select Pacsun stores and online.

UFC BJJ Rebrand: The UFC has rebranded its grappling events from “UFC Fight Pass Invitational” to “UFC BJJ,” adopting a Craig Jones Invitational-style pit and rules. This move signals UFC’s intent to expand its influence in the Brazilian jiu-jitsu scene, with a new reality show and a focus on high-profile grappling matches.

Phorm Energy Drink Partnership: UFC President Dana White, alongside Anheuser-Busch and St. Louis-based 1st Phorm, launched Phorm Energy, a new energy drink with natural flavors and caffeine. This partnership leverages Anheuser-Busch’s distribution network to enhance UFC’s brand reach.

Hpnotiq Marketing Deal: UFC announced a multiyear partnership with Hpnotiq, making the liqueur an Official Partner. Hpnotiq will have prominent branding inside the Octagon during all U.S.-based UFC Fight Nights, tapping into UFC’s global audience of over 700 million fans across 170 countries.

UFC’s Global Growth Recognition: UFC was named one of TIME’s 2025 Most Influential Companies, highlighting its global expansion, including a first-ever event in Azerbaijan and a record-breaking $1.4 billion in revenue in 2024. Dana White emphasized UFC’s universal appeal, stating, “Fighting is in our DNA.”

Drake’s OVO Collaboration: Posts on X indicate that Drake’s OVO brand teased a collaboration with UFC, set to release on June 27, 2025, aligning with International Fight Week. This adds to UFC’s growing list of high-profile brand partnerships. UFC Fitness Equipment: Dyaco, holding the global license for UFC-branded fitness equipment, is promoting “UFC Zones” in gyms worldwide, capitalizing on UFC’s reputation for elite performance and its 300 million-strong fanbase. One of history’s greatest land deals was sealed when a future American president sat face to face with the emperor of France.

In early 1803, President Thomas Jefferson sent James Monroe to Paris to join Robert Livingston. Their mission was to purchase New Orleans and secure American rights on the Mississippi. Napoleon had other plans. Pressed by war with Britain and setbacks in the Caribbean he offered the entire Louisiana Territory instead.

Monroe and Livingston acted at once. On May 2, 1803, they signed the treaty that transferred more than 800,000 square miles to the United States for 15 million dollars. The purchase nearly doubled the size of the young republic in a single stroke.

The day before the signing Monroe met Napoleon at the Louvre. The First Consul greeted him and stated that their affairs should be settled. That brief encounter closed one of the most consequential bargains ever made between the Old World and the New.
